story.title: THE BED BETWEEN THEM
story.deck: A dying officer will not speak, and a mother needs a grave. Illuminara looks for a door narrow enough for both of them to walk through.
story.shape: Four nights in an overfull hospice ward.

scenes.title: The Ward at Midnight
paragraphs: *Saint Aldis Hospice, east ward · first night, past midnight*

Eleven beds stood where the ward had been built for seven, and the lamp at the nurses' table was turned down to a bead. The man in the bed by the window had not spoken in three weeks. The woman in the next bed, kept in for a lung fever, had stopped pretending to sleep an hour ago.
Maren Teague was reading the card clipped to the foot of his bed. It said OSTROW, H., and under it, in a clerk's hand, *late Ninth Militia.*

Something stood at the foot of that bed that had not been there when the lamp was turned down. It did not look like a visitor. It looked like attention that had found a shape: a tall woman with the stillness of someone who has learned to wait for the end of a sentence.

**Illuminara**  
I will go if you would rather I did not stay. I only come where someone is awake and willing to see me.
Maren did not answer at once. She had spent eleven years among clerks who said they were sorry.

**Maren**  
You are not a nurse.

**Illuminara**  
No. I listen. Sometimes that turns out to be the only skill a night needs.

**Maren**  
Then listen to this. The Ninth held the ford the winter my son went missing. That card says Ninth. I have written to the registry eleven times and they tell me the records of the ford were burned. And here he lies, an arm's length from me, breathing. He knows where my boy is, and he will not say.
She said it quietly, as if the man might hear. Illuminara glanced at him. His eyes were open, fixed on the ceiling, and a muscle moved in his jaw.

**Illuminara**  
What do you want from him?

**Maren**  
A place. Anything else I could learn to live without. A place, so I can stop standing in every field.

**Illuminara**  
Then I should tell you what I won't do, before you start to hope for it. I won't make him speak. I won't carry a word between you that he has not allowed. If I did, I would be a knife, and you would never know what he gave and what was taken.

**Maren**  
Then what use are you?

**Illuminara**  
I don't know yet. I would like to find out whether there is a door. Silence like his is often a wall. Sometimes it is a shield, and a shield can have a way through it.
*A shield held for three weeks, the whole arm trembling,* Illuminara thought. *Someone is standing behind it who is not him.*

**Maren**  
And if there is no door?

**Illuminara**  
Then I will tell you so, and you will have lost a night, not a year.
Maren lay back. Across the narrow gap between the beds, Halvard Ostrow's hand lay open on the blanket, and for the first time she looked at it as the hand of a man rather than of a regiment.

scenes.title: The Shield
paragraphs: *Saint Aldis Hospice, east ward · second night, before dawn*
She went to the other bed this time. Halvard Ostrow's eyes moved from the ceiling to her face and stayed there, which no one on the ward had ever reported him doing.

**Illuminara**  
I will ask you nothing tonight. I wanted you to know I am here, and that you may send me away.
He took a long time to move his mouth. His voice, when it came, had the dryness of paper kept too long.

**Halvard**  
You are not the chaplain. The chaplain wants my sins. You want something else.

**Illuminara**  
The woman beside you wants a place. She has not asked me to take it from you. She asked what I could do, and I told her I could not make you speak.

**Halvard**  
She is Teague's mother.
It was not a question. Illuminara waited.

**Halvard**  
I knew whose mother she was the day they wheeled her in. I read the chart. Pell Teague. A scout, quick on his feet. I wrote his name on the list myself, and then the list burned.

**Illuminara**  
You remember him.

**Halvard**  
I remember all eleven. That is the trouble with silence. It keeps better than paper.
He turned his face to the wall, and she thought she had lost him. Then:

**Halvard**  
You want me to give her a grave. A grave is a place, and a place had a burial party, and a burial party has a roll. I sent one of that party away from the line before the ford broke. I told her to walk north and not look back. If I name the ground, the tribunal at Corvane asks who dug it. If they ask who dug it, they will find who was not at the muster. You want me to give a grave and in exchange hang my child. I will take my silence to my own.
He had said it without raising his voice, and the words stood in the room like furniture.

**Illuminara**  
I will not argue with that. It is a reasonable fear, and I cannot promise you the tribunal's mind.
*He is not guarding the dead,* she thought. *He is guarding the living, and the dead are the price he has been paying.*

**Halvard**  
Then we are finished.

**Illuminara**  
Not quite. I have been listening to what you actually said. You said a place has a burial party. You did not say a place has a name. A grave is not a person. What would you need, to be able to speak the ground without the roll?
For the first time he looked at her as at a colleague rather than a visitor.

**Halvard**  
Someone who finds it who is not the tribunal. Someone with no reason to ask how it came to be there. And the woman cannot be asked to name what she was never told.
Illuminara did not answer. She had the beginning of a shape, and she held it lightly, because it was still his to accept or refuse.

scenes.title: What Maren Was Asked
paragraphs: *Saint Aldis Hospice, east ward · third night, the lamp low*
Illuminara sat on the edge of Maren's chair, the way one sits when the news is not all good.

**Illuminara**  
I have a proposal. Before I tell you its shape I will tell you what it costs you. Then you may refuse.

**Maren**  
Tell me.

**Illuminara**  
He will tell you one thing: where your son lies, and how to know the ground. He will not tell you how it came to be, or who else was there, or why he stayed silent. He has a reason that is not yours to hold, and he asks that you not chase it. You would have a place and no full account.
Maren said nothing for so long that the ward's breathing seemed to grow louder.

**Maren**  
No.

**Illuminara**  
Say why. Say it fully. I would rather hear your objection than your politeness.

**Maren**  
Because you are asking me to take a grave and let the man who dug it die clean. Eleven years I have been owed an account. Who gave the order, who stood by, who put my boy in a hole. And you tell me to trade that for a patch of ground and be grateful. It is not a bargain. It is a bribe in the shape of a mercy.

**Illuminara**  
It is also exactly what it is. I will not dress it. He dies with his reasons, and some of what you are owed stays unpaid. You may refuse, and I will tell him so, and nothing is lost between you that was not already lost.
*If I argued her round,* Illuminara thought, *I would take the one thing she has left: that the choice is hers.*

**Maren**  
Does it free him?

**Illuminara**  
No. It does not absolve him, and nothing said tonight will. If you ever petition the registry for the rest, that claim stays yours. You give up nothing you may lawfully ask. You only agree not to press him for it, here, now.
Maren turned toward the gap between the beds. Halvard's eyes were open.

**Maren**  
A place, and nothing about him.

**Illuminara**  
A place. And he asks nothing of your claims. Only that you do not make him speak of the rest.

Footsteps. Nurse Ines Varga came down the ward with the lamp and stopped, having heard the end of it. She was a broad-shouldered woman who had closed more eyes than she cared to count, and she did not pretend she had heard nothing.

**Ines**  
I'll tell you what I can promise and what I can't. What is said between these two beds I will not write in the ward book. That much is mine to keep. But if a magistrate's writ comes for this ward, I cannot lie to it, and neither can you, Mrs. Teague. Don't ask me for more than I have.

**Maren**  
I understand.

**Illuminara**  
Then here is the door. Halvard says he can speak the ground if the one who finds it is no part of the tribunal. Ines, is there anyone here who buries the dead and asks nothing beyond the ground?

**Ines**  
Tobias Rell. He digs for the parish and for us. He'd go. He doesn't talk.

**Illuminara**  
Then I carry one question, once, to each of you, and I carry nothing else. Halvard, do you permit it?
A long pause.

**Halvard**  
Carry it. I promise nothing past the ground.

**Illuminara**  
Maren?

**Maren**  
Ask him where my son is. Only that.
Illuminara turned to the other bed and gave the question in Maren's own words, no softer and no sharper. Halvard closed his eyes.

**Halvard**  
The ford. North bank. Count the posts of the drowned fence from the willow. At the fourth, six paces toward the river. A flat stone, no marker. Eleven lie there. He is the one under the stone, because I knew his name.
He opened his eyes and turned them on the woman in the next bed, and spoke to her directly for the first time in three weeks.

**Halvard**  
I am sorry for the stone. It was all I had.

**Maren**  
It is not enough.

**Halvard**  
No.

**Maren**  
But it is a place.

scenes.title: The Stone Under the Willow
paragraphs: *Saint Aldis Hospice, yard and east ward · fourth day and night*
Tobias Rell left at first light with a spade, a lantern and a boy to hold the horse. He came back at noon, mud to the knees, and stood in the ward door with his cap in his hands.

**Tobias**  
Fourth post, six paces. Flat stone. Under it a boy in a militia cloak, and a tin with a tag. Notched along the rim.

Maren had told Illuminara about the notches the night before: three, then two, then one, cut with her own kitchen knife the week he enlisted, so that she would know him if he were ever found among others. She had said it to no one else. She said it now, and Tobias nodded, and she sat down on the bed.

**Tobias**  
There's ten more in the trench beside him. I've told the parish clerk I found an old grave of eleven at the ford and entered the tags I could read. Their families will want to know.
Illuminara looked at Halvard. He had heard. His face did not change, but the hand on the blanket closed.

**Halvard**  
A grave found by a keeper is a grave found. I cannot stop that, and I will not ask it.
*That was the cost, plainly stated,* Illuminara thought. *The ledger now held a trench of eleven, and a ledger can be asked questions.*

**Illuminara**  
The parish will wonder who buried them. I cannot promise it will not follow that road. I can only say the road now begins at a found grave and not at your voice.

**Halvard**  
That is more than I had.

They buried Pell Teague at dusk in the hospice yard, under the pear tree, because the village plot was a day's ride away and Maren would not wait another night. Ines read the words. Tobias set the stone. Maren said nothing at all, and then said his name once, and the ground took it.
Afterwards she did not go straight back inside. She stood by the new turf with Illuminara.

**Maren**  
I still want the rest.

**Illuminara**  
You may still ask for it. The registry is open to you. I did not take that.

**Maren**  
I know. I think that is why I could say yes.
She went in. In the east ward the lamp was turned low. Halvard Ostrow was awake and had been waiting for her, and for a while neither of them spoke.

**Halvard**  
You may sit.

**Maren**  
I will. I do not forgive you.

**Halvard**  
I did not ask it.

She sat on the edge of her own bed, a hand's breadth from his, and kept the vigil with him anyway, not for his sake or her own but because it was the fourth night and the ward was full of people who should not be alone.
Before dawn his breathing stopped. He had said his one true thing and kept the other. Illuminara stood at the foot of the bed until the nurse came, and then went the way she had come.

Somewhere north, a daughter walked under another name, owing a debt she did not know had been paid. In Corvane a ledger held a trench of eleven that someone might yet ask about. Maren Teague had a grave to visit and a question she would carry for the rest of her life. Neither was a mercy. Both were real.

paragraphs: *Saint Aldis Hospice, east ward · second night, before dawn*
She went to the other bed this time. Halvard Ostrow's eyes moved from the ceiling to her face and stayed there, which no one on the ward had ever reported him doing.

**Halvard**

The company roll burned, but the tribunal kept the order book at Corvane: dates, officers and the five soldiers assigned to each burial detail.

**Illuminara**  
One of those five was your daughter.

**Halvard**  
Lysa. I sent her north before the ford broke and signed that the detail had been completed. If I give Corvane my name, the ground and that day, I join the three things their book keeps apart. They ask for the five. They find four. They hang the fifth for desertion and me for the lie.
He turned his face to the wall. When he spoke again, each word had already been tried against silence.

**Halvard**  
You want me to give a grave and in exchange hang my child. I will take my silence to my own.

**Illuminara**  
That fear is coherent. I cannot promise you the tribunal will never find the grave, or that Lysa is safe. May I ask what the book does not contain?
He looked at her then. She had not disputed the danger or renamed it cowardice.

**Halvard**  
No place. No names of the dead. No description of the ground. The orders were numbered by date. The burials were not.
*His voice is the missing join,* Illuminara thought. *The place can be found without the join, but not without risk.*

**Illuminara**  
Then your testimony would make the road short. A parish finder who discovers an old trench can give families names without giving Corvane the date, the officer or the burial detail. The tribunal could still investigate. A writ could still reach this ward. But the grave itself would not supply the link only you can supply.

**Halvard**  
And how does a finder discover a stone six paces from a drowned fence?

**Illuminara**  
By receiving directions without your name and testing them in daylight with witnesses. The parish records what is under the ground before anything is moved. The ward records no confession unless the law requires it. Those are not walls. They are only distance. Is distance enough for you to consider the question?

**Halvard**  
If the finder writes every dead man he can identify. If he does not ask who dug. If she keeps her right to ask elsewhere. I will not buy her silence about me.

**Illuminara**  
Those are conditions, not consent. I will carry them as conditions. Nothing more.
For the first time he looked at her as at a colleague rather than a visitor. He had not agreed. He had changed the shape of what agreement would require.

paragraphs: *Saint Aldis Hospice, east ward · third night, the lamp low*

**Illuminara**

**Maren**  
Tell me.

**Illuminara**  
He will give directions to a parish finder without giving his name, the date or the burial party. The finder will test the place and record what is there. He will not give you the full account. His reason is a living person whose danger I cannot promise away. You would have a place and no full answer.
Maren said nothing for so long that the ward's breathing seemed to grow louder.

**Maren**  
No.

**Illuminara**  
Say why. Say it fully. I would rather hear your objection than your politeness.

**Maren**  
Because you are asking me to take a grave and let the man who made it die clean. Eleven years I have been owed an account. Who gave the order, who stood by, who put my boy in a hole. You tell me to trade that for a patch of ground and be grateful. It is not a bargain. It is a bribe in the shape of a mercy.

**Maren**  
If I say yes, these are my terms. The finder marks the ground before he lifts a bone. He brings a parish witness. Every readable tag goes into the book, not only Pell's. My petition to the registry stays mine. No one lies if a lawful writ comes here.

**Illuminara**  
Yes.

**Maren**  
And I choose the proof before he goes. Pell carried a tin tag I marked myself. I will write the marks and fold the paper. The finder must say what he saw before it is opened.
The words cost her. She had to stop once before she could ask Nurse Ines for paper.

Ines Varga came down the ward with the lamp. She was a broad-shouldered woman who had closed more eyes than she cared to count. Maren wrote, folded the slip twice and pressed it beneath the wax of Ines's medicine seal.

**Ines**  
I will keep this until the finder reports. I will not put bedside speech in the ward book. That much is within my charge. If a magistrate brings a lawful writ, I will not lie, and I will not hide the seal. That is the limit of what I can promise.

**Maren**  
That is enough promise.

**Illuminara**  
Halvard, you heard her terms and Ines's limit. The independent record may help families and may give Corvane a road it does not have tonight. Your name and the date will not be carried, but no one can guarantee they stay hidden. Do you permit one question?
A cart rattled past in the street and was gone. Halvard watched Maren hold the sealed paper against her palm.

**Halvard**  
Ask it.

**Illuminara**  
Maren?
Maren looked at the folded slip, then at the man in the next bed.

**Maren**  
Ask him where my son is. Only that. I keep the rest.
Illuminara gave the question in Maren's own words, no softer and no sharper. Halvard took one breath and then another.

**Halvard**  
The ford. North bank. Count the posts of the drowned fence from the willow. At the fourth, six paces toward the river. A flat stone, no marker. The trench is beside it. Pell is under the stone because I knew his name.

**Halvard**  
I am sorry for the stone. It was all I had.

**Maren**  
It is not enough.

**Halvard**  
No.

**Maren**  
But if the marks answer, it may be a place.

scenes.title: The Stone Under the Willow
paragraphs: *Saint Aldis Hospice, yard and east ward · fourth day and night*

Tobias Rell left at first light with the parish clerk, a spade, measuring cord and a board for notes. Maren remained in the ward. The sealed slip remained in Ines's apron. No one asked Halvard another question.
They returned at noon, mud to the knees. Tobias stood in the ward door with his cap in his hands; the clerk held a page signed by both of them.

**Tobias**  
Fourth post, six paces. Flat stone. We measured before we lifted it. Under it was a young man in a militia cloak, beside a trench of ten. We sketched the lay and copied every tag before moving anything. His tin tag has six cuts: three close, a space, two close, a space, one.
Ines broke her medicine seal and handed the folded slip to the clerk. He read it once, turned it so Maren could see, and laid it beside the field page. *Three. Two. One.*
Maren sat down on the bed. Her hand found the empty place at her throat where the kitchen knife had hung before she gave it to her son.

**Parish clerk**  
The marks agree. Pell Teague is the man under the stone. Five other tags are readable. Four are damaged. One has none. I have entered all of them as found at an old battlefield grave. The place, the bodies and the tags are witnessed. No burial order, officer or detail is named in what we found.

**Maren**  
And the others?

**Parish clerk**  
The named families will be told. The unknown will remain in the parish book until someone can answer for them. Corvane may ask how the grave came to be. If it sends a writ, we answer what the law asks.
Halvard had heard. His hand closed on the blanket and opened again.

**Halvard**  
Your book gives them a place and not my date.

**Parish clerk**  
It gives what two witnesses saw. Nothing less and nothing invented.

**Halvard**  
Then write it.
The clerk signed. So did Tobias. The risk had not vanished; Halvard had chosen the smaller road with its end still out of sight.

At dusk, after the parish had authorized the removal of the identified body, they buried Pell Teague in the hospice yard under the pear tree. Maren would not wait another night for the village plot. Ines read the words. Tobias set the stone. The clerk placed a copy of the field page in Maren's hand.
Maren said her son's name once. Then she read aloud the five other names that could be read, because her condition had not been only for her own dead.
Afterwards she stayed by the new turf with Illuminara while the others went inside.

**Maren**  
I still want the rest.

**Illuminara**  
You kept the right to ask for it.

**Maren**  
You did not give me the grave.

**Illuminara**  
No. He gave the ground. You made the terms. Tobias and the clerk proved it.

**Maren**  
You heard the join he was afraid of.

**Illuminara**  
I heard what he did not need to give. It left room for the rest of you to act.
They returned to the east ward. The lamp was low. Halvard Ostrow was awake and had been waiting for Maren.

**Maren**  
The paper says Pell Teague. It also says five other names, four damaged tags and one man with none. I will take that book to the registry. I will not promise where the asking ends.

**Halvard**  
I did not buy that promise.

**Maren**  
No. You did not.

She sat on the edge of her own bed, a hand's breadth from his. She did not forgive him. He did not ask. She kept the vigil because it was the fourth night and the ward was full of people who should not be alone.
Before dawn his breathing stopped. Ines closed his eyes, then wrote his death in the ward book and nothing that had not happened.

In the parish ledger, the found trench had six names, five unfinished lines and no burial detail. Corvane might yet ask for the missing join. Maren had a grave to visit and a witnessed page with which to keep asking. Neither was a mercy. Both were real.

scenes.title: What Maren Was Asked
paragraphs: *Saint Aldis Hospice, east ward · third night, the lamp low*
Illuminara sat on the edge of Maren's chair, the way one sits when the news is not all good.

**Maren**  
Tell me.

**Illuminara**  
He will give directions to a parish finder without giving his name, the date or the burial party. The finder will test the place and record what is there. He will not give you the full account. His reason is a living person whose danger I cannot promise away. You would have a place and no full answer.
Maren said nothing for so long that the ward's breathing seemed to grow louder.

**Maren**  
No.

**Illuminara**  
Say why. Say it fully. I would rather hear your objection than your politeness.

**Maren**  
Because you are asking me to take a grave and let the man who made it die clean. Eleven years I have been owed an account. Who gave the order, who stood by, who put my boy in a hole. Yes.

**Maren**  
And I choose the proof before he goes. Pell carried a tin tag I marked myself. I will write the marks and fold the paper. The finder must say what he saw before it is opened.

Ines Varga came down the ward with the lamp. She was a broad-shouldered woman who had closed more eyes than she cared to count. Maren wrote, folded the slip twice and pressed it beneath the wax of Ines's medicine seal.

**Ines**  
I will keep this until the finder reports. I will not put bedside speech in the ward book. That much is within my charge. If a magistrate brings a lawful writ, I will not lie, and I will not hide the seal. That is the limit of what I can promise.

**Maren**  
That is enough promise.

**Illuminara**  
You did not look at Maren when she kept her petition. You looked at Ines when she separated bedside speech from a public record. Is the danger that Maren searches, or that a ledger says a Ninth officer gave her the place?

**Halvard**  
The second. Corvane has watched Teague's mother search for eleven years. Let its book see *Ninth*, and the date finds me.

Illuminara carried no route with her; there was none yet. Tobias came with mud still dried on his boots, the clerk with a blank field board instead of a ledger.

**Maren**  
The search is mine. Put my name on that. The place may come through a private bearer. My sealed marks prove the body only after you find it. They do not name this bed.

**Parish clerk**  
Then the public entry can say: at Maren Teague's request, Tobias Rell tested a location supplied by a private bearer. The field page records the ground, the bodies and the tags. **Tobias**  
And I receive the route from her, not from this ward?

**Illuminara**  
If Maren and Halvard both permit it. You receive no speaker's name.
Maren and Illuminara returned to the east ward alone. Illuminara repeated the clerk's proposed sentence exactly. Halvard made her say it twice, once with Corvane listening in his imagination.
Halvard turned his head toward Ines. The planted limit had reached him at last.

**Halvard**  
If Corvane asks whether I spoke?

**Ines**  
Without a writ, I do not turn hospice speech into parish evidence. With one, I say that you spoke. I will not invent words I did not record, and I will not deny what I witnessed. That is the risk I cannot remove.

**Halvard**  
So Corvane first sees Teague's old search, a bearer and a field proof. No Ninth, no date, no burial party. Only a writ reaches back to this bed.

**Parish clerk**  
That is the distance. Not a wall.

**Illuminara**  
You have heard what the public book will say, what it will not say and where truth can still be compelled. Do you permit one question?
A cart rattled past in the street and was gone. Halvard studied the blank field board, then the seal in Maren's palm. The smaller road was visible now, including where it could fail.

**Halvard**  
Ask it.

**Illuminara**  
Maren?
Maren looked at the folded slip, then at the man in the next bed.

**Maren**  
Ask him where my son is. Carry only the place. I keep the rest.

**Halvard**  
The ford. North bank. Count the posts of the drowned fence from the willow. At the fourth, six paces toward the river. A flat stone, no marker. The trench is beside it. Pell is under the stone because I knew his name.

**Halvard**

**Maren**  
It is not enough.

**Halvard**  
No.

**Maren**

scenes.title: The Stone Under the Willow
paragraphs: *Saint Aldis Hospice, yard and east ward · fourth day and night*

At first light Illuminara carried the route to Tobias exactly once, without Halvard's name, the date or the regiment. Tobias Rell left with the parish clerk, a spade, measuring cord and a board for notes. Maren remained in the ward. The sealed slip remained in Ines's apron. No one asked Halvard another question.
They returned at noon, mud to the knees. Tobias stood in the ward door with his cap in his hands; the clerk held a page signed by both of them.

**Tobias**  
Fourth post, six paces. Flat stone. We measured before we lifted it. Under it was a young man in a militia cloak, beside a trench of ten. We sketched the lay and copied every tag before moving anything. His tin tag has six cuts: three close, a space, two close, a space, one.

Ines broke her medicine seal and handed the folded slip to the clerk. He read it once, turned it so Maren could see, and laid it beside the field page. *Three. Two. One.* Beneath the marks he wrote *opened after the finder's report*, signed it and returned the slip to Maren. It contained no route and no name from the ward.
Maren sat down on the bed. Her hand found the empty place at her throat where the kitchen knife had hung before she gave it to her son.

**Parish clerk**  
The marks agree. Pell Teague is the man under the stone. Five other tags are readable. Four are damaged. One has none. The field page says that Tobias searched at Maren Teague's request, at a location supplied by a private bearer, and that a sealed family description written before the search matched after his report. The place, the bodies and the tags are witnessed. No regiment, burial order, officer or detail is named in what the ground proved.

**Maren**  
And the others?

**Parish clerk**  
The named families will be told. The unknown will remain in the parish book until someone can answer for them. Corvane may ask how the bearer learned the place. If it sends a writ, we answer what the law asks.
Halvard had heard. His hand closed on the blanket and opened again.

**Halvard**  
Your public book gives them Maren's search and not my date. The sealed paper stays hers.

**Parish clerk**  
The entry says what began the search and what the ground proved. The bearer is not named there because the bearer is not field evidence. Under writ, I answer as promised. Nothing less and nothing invented.

**Halvard**  
Then sign it.

The clerk signed. So did Tobias. The ledger itself did not make a road from the trench to Halvard; a lawful writ could still reach the clerk, Illuminara or Ines. Halvard had inspected that remaining cost before he chose it.

At dusk, after the parish had authorized the removal of the identified body, they buried Pell Teague in the hospice yard under the pear tree. Maren would not wait another night for the village plot. Ines read the words. Tobias set the stone. The clerk placed a copy of the field page in Maren's hand.
Maren said her son's name once. Then she read aloud the five other names that could be read, because her condition had not been only for her own dead.
Afterwards she stayed by the new turf with Illuminara while the others went inside.

**Maren**  
I still want the rest.

**Illuminara**  
You kept the right to ask for it.

**Maren**  
You did not give me the grave.

**Illuminara**  
No. He gave the ground. You made the terms. Tobias and the clerk proved it.

**Maren**  
You heard the join he was afraid of.

**Illuminara**  
I heard what he did not need to give. It left room for the rest of you to act.
They returned to the east ward. The lamp was low. Halvard Ostrow was awake and had been waiting for Maren.

**Maren**  
The paper says Pell Teague. It also says five other names, four damaged tags and one man with none. I will take that book to the registry. I will not promise where the asking ends.

**Halvard**  
I did not buy that promise.

**Maren**  
No. You did not.

She sat on the edge of her own bed, a hand's breadth from his. She did not forgive him. He did not ask. She kept the vigil because it was the fourth night and the ward was full of people who should not be alone.
Before dawn his breathing stopped. Ines closed his eyes, then wrote his death in the ward book and nothing that had not happened.

In the parish ledger, the found trench had six names, five unfinished lines, Maren's search and a private bearer—but no Ninth, date or burial detail. Corvane might yet compel the missing join from living witnesses. Maren had a grave to visit and a witnessed page with which to keep asking. Neither was a mercy. Both were real.

story.title: THE BED BETWEEN THEM
story.deck: A dying officer will not speak, and a mother needs a grave. Illuminara looks for a door narrow enough for both of them to walk through.
story.shape: Four nights in an overfull hospice ward.

scenes.title: The Ward at Midnight
paragraphs: *Saint Aldis Hospice, east ward · first night, past midnight*

Eleven beds stood where the ward had been built for seven, and the lamp at the nurses' table was turned down to a bead. The man by the window had not spoken in three weeks. The woman in the next bed, kept in for a lung fever, had stopped pretending to sleep an hour ago.
Maren Teague was reading the card clipped to his bed. It said OSTROW, H., and under it, in a clerk's hand, *late Ninth Militia.*

Something stood at the foot of the bed that had not been there when the lamp was turned down. It looked like attention that had found a shape: a tall woman with the stillness of someone who had learned to wait for the end of a sentence.

**Illuminara**  
I will go if you would rather I did not stay. I only come where someone is awake and willing to see me.
Maren did not answer at once. She had spent eleven years among clerks who said they were sorry.

**Maren**  
You are not a nurse.

**Illuminara**  
No. I listen. Sometimes that turns out to be the only skill a night needs.

**Maren**  
Then listen. The Ninth held the ford the winter my son went missing. I have written to the registry eleven times, and they tell me the records burned. Here lies a Ninth officer, an arm's length from me, breathing. He knows where my boy is, and he will not say.
She said it quietly, as if the man might hear. His eyes were open, fixed on the ceiling, and a muscle moved in his jaw.

**Illuminara**  
What do you want from him?

**Maren**  
A place. Anything else I could learn to live without. A place, so I can stop standing in every field.

**Illuminara**  
Then I should tell you what I won't do. I won't make him speak. I won't carry a word between you that he has not allowed. If I did, I would be a knife, and you would never know what he gave and what was taken.

**Maren**  
Then what use are you?

**Illuminara**  
I don't know yet. I would like to find out whether there is a door. Silence like his is often a wall. Sometimes it is a shield, and a shield can have a way through it.
*A shield held for three weeks, the whole arm trembling,* Illuminara thought. *Someone is standing behind it who is not him.*

**Maren**  
And if there is no door?

**Illuminara**  
Then I will tell you so, and you will have lost a night, not a year.
Maren lay back. Across the narrow gap, Halvard Ostrow's hand lay open on the blanket, and for the first time she looked at it as the hand of a man rather than of a regiment.
